We find that reasoning token length expands as performance improves, peaks at the stage of conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task. Notably, after training, models retain performance even when reasoning is removed--suggesting it scaffolded learning but is no longer needed. This progression offers actionable insights: reasoning token dynamics can serve as a signal for diagnosing training stage, identifying convergence, and guiding early stopping. We propose metrics to track this trajectory and argue that reasoning behavior is valuable for understanding and optimizing reasoning model training.

papers.title: Transformers Provably Learn Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Length Generalization
papers.research_question: Can transformers, trained via gradient descent, learn chain-of-thought reasoning to solve problems requiring inherently sequential reasoning beyond TC0? Can the learned reasoning ability generalize to problems that require longer chain-of-thoughts beyond the lengths of training data?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that one-layer transformers trained with gradient descent can learn chain-of-thought reasoning for state-tracking tasks, with length generalization governed by the algebraic structure of the group actions, and introduces a recursive self-training scheme to extend solvable problem lengths.
papers.conclusion: The paper proves that transformers can learn chain-of-thought reasoning with length generalization, with generalization behavior dictated by the algebraic structure of the task, and shows that recursive self-training can extend solvable lengths.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can provably learn to solve state-tracking problems via chain-of-thought reasoning.
For simply transitive group actions, chain-of-thought training on constant-length problems generalizes to much longer lengths.
For symmetry group actions, length generalization is limited to a constant factor of the training length.
A recursive self-training scheme can bootstrap the solvable problem length to maximal allowable length.
Constant-depth transformers can learn to solve NC1-complete problems, going beyond TC0.
papers.abstract: The ability to reason lies at the core of artificial intelligence (AI), and challenging problems usually call for deeper and longer reasoning to tackle. A crucial question about AI reasoning is whether models can extrapolate learned reasoning patterns to solve harder tasks with longer chain-of-thought (CoT). In this work, we present a theoretical analysis of transformers learning on synthetic state-tracking tasks with gradient descent. We mathematically prove how the algebraic structure of state-tracking problems governs the degree of extrapolation of the learned CoT. Specifically, our theory characterizes the length generalization of transformers through the mechanism of attention concentration, linking the retrieval robustness of the attention layer to the state-tracking task structure of long-context reasoning. Moreover, for transformers with limited reasoning length, we prove that a recursive self-training scheme can progressively extend the range of solvable problem lengths. To our knowledge, we provide the first optimization guarantee that constant-depth transformers provably learn $\mathsf{NC}^1$-complete problems with CoT, significantly going beyond prior art confined in $\mathsf{TC}^0$, unless the widely held conjecture $\mathsf{TC}^0 \neq \mathsf{NC}^1$ fails. Finally, we present a broad set of experiments supporting our theoretical results, confirming the length generalization behaviors and the mechanism of attention concentration.

papers.title: LM2: Large Memory Models
papers.research_question: How can we enhance Transformer architectures with an explicit memory module to improve long-context reasoning and multi-step inference without degrading general task performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LM2, a memory-augmented Transformer architecture with a dynamic memory module that enhances long-context reasoning and multi-step inference while maintaining or improving performance on general tasks.
papers.conclusion: The LM2 architecture demonstrates the importance of explicit memory mechanisms in Transformers, providing a foundation for further research on long-term memory in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
LM2 outperforms baseline models (RMT and Llama-3.2) on the BABILong benchmark by large margins (37.1% and 86.3% on average).
LM2 achieves a 5.0% improvement on MMLU over a pre-trained vanilla model, showing that the memory module does not harm general task performance.
Integrating memory modules in more decoder blocks leads to lower perplexity and better performance.
Analysis of memory slots shows that they specialize in different types of information (e.g., factual retrieval, structural cues).
Test-time memory updates adaptively focus on relevant tokens for the task.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the Large Memory Model (LM2), a decoder-only Transformer architecture enhanced with an auxiliary memory module that aims to address the limitations of standard Transformers in multi-step reasoning, relational argumentation, and synthesizing information distributed over long contexts. The proposed LM2 incorporates a memory module that acts as a contextual representation repository, interacting with input tokens via cross attention and updating through gating mechanisms. To preserve the Transformers general-purpose capabilities, LM2 maintains the original information flow while integrating a complementary memory pathway. Experimental results on the BABILong benchmark demonstrate that the LM2model outperforms both the memory-augmented RMT model by 37.1% and the baseline Llama-3.2 model by 86.3% on average across tasks. LM2 exhibits exceptional capabilities in multi-hop inference, numerical reasoning, and large-context question-answering. On the MMLU dataset, it achieves a 5.0% improvement over a pre-trained vanilla model, demonstrating that its memory module does not degrade performance on general tasks. Further, in our analysis, we explore the memory interpretability, effectiveness of memory modules, and test-time behavior. Our findings emphasize the importance of explicit memory in enhancing Transformer architectures.

papers.title: Mechanism and Emergence of Stacked Attention Heads in Multi-Layer Transformers
papers.research_question: What tasks require transformers of a specific depth? Can large language models solve such tasks without fine-tuning? What mechanism do transformers use to solve the task? How does this mechanism emerge during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the retrieval problem, a task requiring a minimum number of transformer layers, and uncovers that transformers solve it using stacked attention heads (retrieval heads) which emerge gradually via an implicit curriculum.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces the retrieval problem, shows it requires a certain number of layers, and finds transformers solve it using a mechanism resembling an induction head that emerges gradually with the help of an implicit curriculum.
papers.key_findings:
The retrieval problem requires a minimum number of transformer layers that grows logarithmically with the number of retrieval steps.
Large language models can solve the retrieval problem without any specific fine-tuning.
Transformers solve the retrieval problem using stacked attention heads that resemble induction heads.
Retrieval heads emerge gradually during training, one head at a time, guided by an implicit curriculum.
The implicit curriculum is essential for successful learning of the retrieval problem.
papers.limitation:
The analysis of transformers trained on a minimal formulation of the retrieval problem might not generalize perfectly to large language models.
The paper does not provide a full explanation of the training dynamics of transformers on the retrieval problem.
future_direction: Further research is needed to fully understand the multi-layered circuits learned by large language models and the training dynamics that enable their learning.
papers.abstract: In this paper, I introduce the retrieval problem, a simple yet common reasoning task that can be solved only by transformers with a minimum number of layers, which grows logarithmically with the input size. I empirically show that large language models can solve the task under different prompting formulations without any fine-tuning. To understand how transformers solve the retrieval problem, I train several transformers on a minimal formulation. Successful learning occurs only under the presence of an implicit curriculum. I uncover the learned mechanisms by studying the attention maps in the trained transformers. I also study the training process, uncovering that attention heads always emerge in a specific sequence guided by the implicit curriculum.

papers.title: Circuit Compositions: Exploring Modular Structures in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent do neural networks implement reusable functions through subnetworks that can be composed to perform more complex tasks? Specifically, how do circuits for functionally related tasks relate to each other in terms of node overlap and cross-task faithfulness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces activation pruning through continuous sparsification to automatically discover faithful and minimal circuits for sequence-to-sequence tasks, analyzes the modularity of circuits for functionally related string-edit operations, and demonstrates that circuits can be composed via set operations to represent more complex functions.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates a method for circuit discovery and shows that circuits for compositional tasks exhibit modularity and can be composed, providing insights into the modular structure of transformer-based language models.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits identified by activation pruning are both faithful and minimal.
Functionally similar circuits exhibit notable node overlap and cross-task faithfulness.
Circuits can be combined through set operations (e.g., union) to create subnetworks that perform more complex tasks.
papers.limitation:
The method does not guarantee completeness of circuits.
The identified circuits depend on the ablation paradigm (mean vs. zero ablation).
Findings are based on a small model and controlled dataset, and may not generalize to larger models and more complex tasks.
future_direction: Explore more efficient ways to quantify completeness and incorporate it into the optimization framework.
Scale the findings to larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: Memory Injections: Correcting Multi-Hop Reasoning Failures during Inference in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: What causes multi-hop reasoning failures in transformer-based language models, and how can they be corrected during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that attention heads in LLMs fail to recall relevant memories for multi-hop reasoning, and proposes a memory injection method to correct these failures during inference, improving model performance.
papers.conclusion: Memory injections during inference can rectify multi-hop reasoning failures by enhancing recall of relevant information, offering an efficient alternative to retraining or fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads are responsible for memory retrieval in transformers, and their failure leads to multi-hop reasoning errors.
Memory injections into specific attention layers can significantly increase the probability of correct next tokens, by up to 424%.
There are optimal layers and magnitudes for memory injections, which vary by model and dataset.
Curated memories (relevant to the prompt) are more effective than random injections from unrelated parts of speech.
Injections from different parts of speech have varying effects, with conjunctions often performing better due to their neutral role.
papers.limitation:
Internal biases of the question writers and rigid prompt structure limit dataset representativeness
Small size of hand-generated dataset compared to programmatically generated one
Analyses limited to GPT2 models; need to verify on other models
Reliance on unembedding matrix for interpreting hidden states may not be optimal
future_direction: Use memory injections to correct stale or incorrect information, remove private or harmful information, and combat bias during LLM inference.
Automate memory selection via unsupervised algorithms or by connecting LLMs with knowledge bases.
papers.abstract: Answering multi-hop reasoning questions requires retrieving and synthesizing information from diverse sources. Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to perform such reasoning consistently. Here we propose an approach to pinpoint and rectify multi-hop reasoning failures through targeted memory injections on LLM attention heads. First, we analyze the per-layer activations of GPT-2 models in response to single and multi-hop prompts. We then propose a mechanism that allows users to inject pertinent prompt-specific information, which we refer to as "memories," at critical LLM locations during inference. By thus enabling the LLM to incorporate additional relevant information during inference, we enhance the quality of multi-hop prompt completions. We show empirically that a simple, efficient, and targeted memory injection into a key attention layer can often increase the probability of the desired next token in multi-hop tasks, by up to 424%.

papers.title: An Investigation of Neuron Activation as a Unified Lens to Explain Chain-of-Thought Eliciting Arithmetic Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: How can neuron activation in feed-forward layers of LLMs provide a unified explanation for the importance of various components in Chain-of-Thought prompts for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that analyzing the activation of reasoning neurons in feed-forward layers provides a unified explanation for why certain components (e.g., equations, textual explanation) in Chain-of-Thought prompts are important for eliciting arithmetic reasoning in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Neuron activation analysis provides valuable insights into the internal mechanism of LLMs for arithmetic reasoning and can explain prior empirical observations about Chain-of-Thought prompting.
papers.key_findings:
The paper discovered 113 neurons in Llama2-7B associated with arithmetic reasoning concepts such as logical connectors and arithmetic operations.
Corrupting the discovered reasoning neurons via random noise ablation leads to a significant performance drop, demonstrating their importance for eliciting reasoning.
The presence of equations and textual explanation in CoT prompts leads to higher activation of reasoning neurons, explaining their importance for performance.
Diversity of arithmetic operators in prompts leads to activation of a broader set of reasoning neurons, which improves model performance.
Incorrect in-distribution labels do not substantially affect reasoning neuron activation, while out-of-distribution labels cause different activation patterns and lower performance.
papers.limitation:
Neuron activation is necessary but not sufficient to completely explain LLM reasoning; interactions among components are also important.
The seven pre-defined concepts used may not cover the full scope of arithmetic reasoning, and activation can be faked by prompting.
Analysis was performed primarily on Llama2-7B; generalization to other LLMs may require different approaches.
future_direction: Future work should combine neuron activation analysis with other approaches like circuit analysis and top-down methods for a more complete understanding.
Extend the research to other LLMs and more comprehensive sets of reasoning concepts.
Systematically explore the potential of predicting LLM reasoning performance via neuron activation without human labels.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong arithmetic reasoning capabilities when prompted with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompts. However, we have only a limited understanding of how they are processed by LLMs. To demystify it, prior work has primarily focused on ablating different components in the CoT prompt and empirically observing their resulting LLM performance change. Yet, the reason why these components are important to LLM reasoning is not explored. To fill this gap, in this work, we investigate ``neuron activation'' as a lens to provide a unified explanation to observations made by prior work. Specifically, we look into neurons within the feed-forward layers of LLMs that may have activated their arithmetic reasoning capabilities, using Llama2 as an example. To facilitate this investigation, we also propose an approach based on GPT-4 to automatically identify neurons that imply arithmetic reasoning. Our analyses revealed that the activation of reasoning neurons in the feed-forward layers of an LLM can explain the importance of various components in a CoT prompt, and future research can extend it for a more complete understanding.

papers.title: Disentangling and Integrating Relational and Sensory Information in Transformer Architectures
papers.research_question: How can we improve relational reasoning in Transformer architectures by explicitly disentangling and integrating sensory and relational information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Dual Attention Transformer (DAT), an architectural extension that introduces separate sensory and relational attention mechanisms, leading to improved data and parameter efficiency across diverse tasks.
papers.conclusion: Integrating explicit relational attention mechanisms into the Transformer architecture improves performance and efficiency across a range of tasks, including relational reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, image recognition, and language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
DAT is more sample-efficient than standard Transformers on synthetic relational reasoning tasks.
DAT outperforms standard Transformers on mathematical problem-solving tasks across model sizes.
DAT achieves higher accuracy than standard Vision Transformers on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 image classification.
DAT language models achieve lower perplexity than standard Transformers on the FineWeb-Edu dataset.
papers.abstract: Relational reasoning is a central component of generally intelligent systems, enabling robust and data-efficient inductive generalization. Recent empirical evidence shows that many existing neural architectures, including Transformers, struggle with tasks requiring relational reasoning. In this work, we distinguish between two types of information: sensory information about the properties of individual objects, and relational information about the relationships between objects. While neural attention provides a powerful mechanism for controlling the flow of sensory information between objects, the Transformer lacks an explicit computational mechanism for routing and processing relational information. To address this limitation, we propose an architectural extension of the Transformer framework that we call the Dual Attention Transformer (DAT), featuring two distinct attention mechanisms: sensory attention for directing the flow of sensory information, and a novel relational attention mechanism for directing the flow of relational information. We empirically evaluate DAT on a diverse set of tasks ranging from synthetic relational benchmarks to complex real-world tasks such as language modeling and visual processing. Our results demonstrate that integrating explicit relational computational mechanisms into the Transformer architecture leads to significant performance gains in terms of data efficiency and parameter efficiency.

papers.title: Demystifying Reasoning Dynamics with Mutual Information: Thinking Tokens are Information Peaks in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What are the critical reasoning steps or intermediate states that significantly affect the final results in the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that during the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs), certain steps exhibit sudden increases in mutual information (MI) with the correct answer, and these MI peaks correspond to 'thinking tokens' (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait') that are critical for reasoning performance. Based on this, the paper proposes two training-free methods to improve reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that thinking tokens, which correspond to MI peaks, are crucial for LRM reasoning and that leveraging these tokens can improve reasoning performance without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
During LRM reasoning, certain steps show sudden and significant increases in mutual information (MI) with the golden answer, termed MI peaks.
The tokens at MI peaks are often reflective or transitional words (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait', 'So') and are critical for reasoning performance; suppressing them significantly harms performance.
Theoretically, higher cumulative MI between representations and the golden answer leads to tighter bounds on prediction error.
Non-reasoning LLMs do not exhibit clear MI peaks, suggesting the phenomenon is a result of reasoning-intensive training.
Two proposed methods, Representation Recycling (RR) and Thinking Token based Test-time Scaling (TTTS), which leverage thinking tokens, can improve reasoning performance on math benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in complex problem-solving, yet their internal reasoning mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the reasoning trajectories of LRMs from an information-theoretic perspective. By tracking how mutual information (MI) between intermediate representations and the correct answer evolves during LRM reasoning, we observe an interesting MI peaks phenomenon: the MI at specific generative steps exhibits a sudden and significant increase during LRM's reasoning process. We theoretically analyze such phenomenon and show that as MI increases, the probability of model's prediction error decreases. Furthermore, these MI peaks often correspond to tokens expressing reflection or transition, such as ``Hmm'', ``Wait'' and ``Therefore,'' which we term as the thinking tokens. We then demonstrate that these thinking tokens are crucial for LRM's reasoning performance, while other tokens has minimal impacts. Building on these analyses, we propose two simple yet effective methods to improve LRM's reasoning performance, by delicately leveraging these thinking tokens. Overall, our work provides novel insights into the reasoning mechanisms of LRMs and offers practical ways to improve their reasoning capabilities. The code is available at https://github.com/ChnQ/MI-Peaks.

papers.title: Scaling Reasoning Hop Exposes Weaknesses: Demystifying and Improving Hop Generalization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates where errors occur in reasoning hop generalization (RQ1) and why these errors arise (RQ2), focusing on the internal mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Test-time Correction of Reasoning (TCR), a lightweight intervention method that dynamically identifies and deactivates erroneous processing heads to improve reasoning hop generalization, based on mechanistic insights into internal competition mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that TCR effectively improves reasoning hop generalization by dynamically deactivating erroneous processing heads, demonstrating the potential of test-time interventions based on mechanistic insights.
papers.key_findings:
Errors in reasoning hop generalization are dominated by token-level erroneous predictions of a few specific error types, enabling focused diagnosis.
These token-level errors stem from an internal competition mechanism: correct trajectories coexist with erroneous ones but are actively suppressed by erroneous processing heads; knocking out such heads can restore correct predictions.
The proposed TCR method, which automatically and dynamically deactivates erroneous processing heads, consistently improves reasoning hop generalization across tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has become the standard paradigm for enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve complex problems. However, recent studies reveal a sharp performance drop in reasoning hop generalization scenarios, where the required number of reasoning steps exceeds training distributions while the underlying algorithm remains unchanged. The internal mechanisms driving this failure remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct a systematic study on tasks from multiple domains, and find that errors concentrate at token positions of a few critical error types, rather than being uniformly distributed. Closer inspection reveals that these token-level erroneous predictions stem from internal competition mechanisms: certain attention heads, termed erroneous processing heads (ep heads), tip the balance by amplifying incorrect reasoning trajectories while suppressing correct ones. Notably, removing individual ep heads during inference can often restore the correct predictions. Motivated by these insights, we propose test-time correction of reasoning, a lightweight intervention method that dynamically identifies and deactivates ep heads in the reasoning process. Extensive experiments across different tasks and LLMs show that it consistently improves reasoning hop generalization, highlighting both its effectiveness and potential.

papers.title: Improving Chain-of-Thought for Logical Reasoning via Attention-Aware Intervention
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode and utilize structural information in their latent representations for logical reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Attention-Aware Intervention (AAI), a non-interactive, end-to-end framework that reweights attention scores to steer LLMs' reasoning for improved logical reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: AAI effectively improves logical reasoning in LLMs by reweighting attention scores based on identified patterns, achieving competitive performance with low overhead.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in LLMs exhibit structured activation patterns (anchor, aggregation, copy heads) when symbolic structures are injected into prompts.
Attention-Aware Intervention (AAI) reweights attention scores to reinforce linkages between rule identifiers and their content, improving reasoning.
AAI improves accuracy on logical reasoning benchmarks like ProofWriter, ProntoQA, Logical Deduction, and FOLIO across various LLMs.
The method scales well with model size and generalizes to mathematical reasoning tasks like GSM8k.
AAI incurs negligible additional computational overhead during inference.
papers.abstract: Modern logical reasoning with LLMs primarily relies on employing complex interactive frameworks that decompose the reasoning process into subtasks solved through carefully designed prompts or requiring external resources (e.g., symbolic solvers) to exploit their strong logical structures. While interactive approaches introduce additional overhead or depend on external components, which limit their scalability. In this work, we introduce a non-interactive, end-to-end framework for reasoning tasks, enabling reasoning to emerge within the model itself-improving generalization while preserving analyzability without any external resources. We show that introducing structural information into the few-shot prompt activates a subset of attention heads that patterns aligned with logical reasoning operators. Building on this insight, we propose Attention-Aware Intervention (AAI), an inference-time intervention method that reweights attention scores across selected heads identified by their logical patterns. AAI offers an efficient way to steer the model's reasoning toward leveraging prior knowledge through attention modulation. Extensive experiments show that AAI enhances logical reasoning performance across diverse benchmarks, and model architectures, while incurring negligible additional computational overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/phuongnm94/aai_for_logical_reasoning.

papers.title: Selection-Inference: Exploiting Large Language Models for Interpretable Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the multi-step logical reasoning capabilities of large language models while producing interpretable, causal reasoning traces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Selection-Inference (SI) framework, which decomposes logical reasoning into iterative selection and inference steps using frozen LLMs, significantly improving performance on multi-step reasoning tasks and producing causal, interpretable reasoning traces.
papers.conclusion: The Selection-Inference framework effectively improves the logical reasoning capabilities of LLMs by breaking down problems into iterative selection and inference steps, yielding both performance gains and interpretable, causal reasoning traces.
papers.key_findings:
Vanilla LLMs perform well on single-step inference but struggle with multi-step logical reasoning.
The SI framework with a 7B LLM almost triples the performance of the same model used naively and outperforms a 40x larger 280B LLM baseline on a suite of logical reasoning tasks.
The SI framework produces causal, natural language reasoning traces that justify the final answer, aiding interpretability and trust.
The modular design of SI allows for error recovery and human inspection of intermediate reasoning steps.
Fine-tuning the Selection and Inference modules on single reasoning steps further improves performance beyond prompt engineering.
papers.limitation:
The main point of failure tends to be the Selection module, which is difficult to quantify without labeled data for intermediate steps.
The approach assumes a database of facts or rules is given, which may not be available in practical settings requiring knowledge retrieval.
The model uses a fixed compute budget (number of steps) and lacks a mechanism for deciding when to halt the reasoning process or filtering reasoning traces.
future_direction: Combine the SI model with knowledge retrieval methods to relax the assumption of given context.
Address the halting problem and develop mechanisms to filter reasoning traces and select the best answer.
Explore fine-tuning the modules for specific tasks to improve performance beyond prompt engineering.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to be capable of impressive few-shot generalisation to new tasks. However, they still tend to perform poorly on multi-step logical reasoning problems. Here we carry out a comprehensive evaluation of LLMs on 50 tasks that probe different aspects of logical reasoning. We show that language models tend to perform fairly well at single step inference or entailment tasks, but struggle to chain together multiple reasoning steps to solve more complex problems. In light of this, we propose a Selection-Inference (SI) framework that exploits pre-trained LLMs as general processing modules, and alternates between selection and inference to generate a series of interpretable, casual reasoning steps leading to the final answer. We show that a 7B parameter LLM used within the SI framework in a 5-shot generalisation setting, with no fine-tuning, yields a performance improvement of over 100% compared to an equivalent vanilla baseline on a suite of 10 logical reasoning tasks. The same model in the same setting even outperforms a significantly larger 280B parameter baseline on the same suite of tasks. Moreover, answers produced by the SI framework are accompanied by a causal natural-language-based reasoning trace, which has important implications for the safety and trustworthiness of the system.

papers.title: A Multiscale Visualization of Attention in the Transformer Model
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a multiscale visualization tool for attention in the Transformer model, demonstrated on BERT and GPT-2, with example use cases.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces a tool for visualizing attention in the Transformer at multiple scales and demonstrates its use on GPT-2 and BERT with three example use cases.
papers.key_findings:
The tool can detect model bias, such as gender bias in coreference resolution in GPT-2.
The tool helps locate relevant attention heads for specific tasks, such as inter-sentence attention for paraphrase detection in BERT.
The neuron view links individual neurons to model behavior, such as identifying neurons responsible for distance-decaying attention patterns.
future_direction: Develop a unified interface to navigate all three views within the tool.
Expose other components of the model, such as the value vectors and state activations.
Enable users to manipulate the model, either by modifying attention or editing individual neurons.
papers.abstract: The Transformer is a sequence model that forgoes traditional recurrent architectures in favor of a fully attention-based approach. Besides improving performance, an advantage of using attention is that it can also help to interpret a model by showing how the model assigns weight to different input elements. However, the multi-layer, multi-head attention mechanism in the Transformer model can be difficult to decipher. To make the model more accessible, we introduce an open-source tool that visualizes attention at multiple scales, each of which provides a unique perspective on the attention mechanism. We demonstrate the tool on BERT and OpenAI GPT-2 and present three example use cases: detecting model bias, locating relevant attention heads, and linking neurons to model behavior.

papers.title: Understanding Hidden Computations in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do transformer models internally process and represent reasoning steps when Chain-of-Thought is replaced with filler characters, and can these hidden characters be recovered?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that hidden characters in filler Chain-of-Thought sequences can be recovered by analyzing layer-wise representations and token rankings without loss of performance, providing insights into internal mechanisms of transformer models.
papers.conclusion: The analysis sheds light on how models internally process and represent reasoning steps when explicit chain of thought is obscured, contributing to model interpretability and opening avenues for improving transparency in language model reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-wise analysis reveals that filler tokens emerge in later layers, overwriting earlier numerical representations.
Token ranking analysis shows that original reasoning tokens remain among lower-ranked candidates beneath filler tokens.
A modified decoding algorithm can recover hidden characters by selecting non-filler tokens when fillers are top-ranked, without compromising task performance.
The model performs necessary computations in earlier layers and then overwrites intermediate representations with filler tokens in later layers to match training targets.
The findings suggest that models retain hidden reasoning steps internally even when outputting filler tokens.
papers.limitation: Focuses on a synthetic task (3SUM) and a relatively small transformer model, which may not capture complexities of real-world language tasks and larger models.
future_direction: Explore whether specific circuits, such as induction heads or particular attention patterns, are involved in overwriting behavior.
Apply similar analysis techniques to other tasks and models to assess the generality of the findings.
Extend the investigation to natural language tasks and larger models to determine if observed phenomena persist in more complex settings.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has significantly enhanced the reasoning abilities of large language models. However, recent studies have shown that models can still perform complex reasoning tasks even when the CoT is replaced with filler(hidden) characters (e.g., "..."), leaving open questions about how models internally process and represent reasoning steps. In this paper, we investigate methods to decode these hidden characters in transformer models trained with filler CoT sequences. By analyzing layer-wise representations using the logit lens method and examining token rankings, we demonstrate that the hidden characters can be recovered without loss of performance. Our findings provide insights into the internal mechanisms of transformer models and open avenues for improving interpretability and transparency in language model reasoning.

papers.title: Investigating Transformer-Guided Chaining for Interpretable Natural Logic Reasoning
papers.research_question: What are the strengths and weaknesses of the transformer guided chaining approach for multi-step natural logic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: An empirical investigation of the transformer guided chaining approach for multi-step natural logic reasoning, showing it achieves human-level performance on a challenging FOL benchmark but has limitations in interpretability and handling certain logical constructs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer guided chaining approach is promising for faithful, interpretable multi-hop reasoning, but current limitations in handling certain FOLs and sub-optimal chain generation suggest areas for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Human-level multi-step reasoning performance is achieved (84.5% machine vs 77.5% human) with a minimalist transformer guided chaining implementation.
The approach requires high accuracy in 1-step inferences; small errors can propagate and magnify over iterations.
FOLs with simple conjunctions and existential quantifiers are easier to handle, whereas FOLs with equivalence are harder, especially with universal quantifiers and disjunctions.
The predicted reasoning chains are correct 78% of the time but could be more than twice longer than the optimal chains.
The t5-base model version was comparable in performance to the t5-large version, suggesting promise for low-compute implementations.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation of interpretability is preliminary, based on a limited human study.
Unable to rigorously analyze the model's ability in handling negations due to dataset complexity.
Evaluation focused on a synthetic dataset; more rigorous evaluation on real-life datasets is needed.
future_direction: Investigating how errors in 1-step inferences propagate and impact chaining performance.
Handling incomplete or inconsistent facts during reasoning.
Extending to more sophisticated inference relations beyond entailment (e.g., necessity, possibility, rebuttal).
papers.abstract: Natural logic reasoning has received increasing attention lately, with several datasets and neural models proposed, though with limited success. More recently, a new class of works have emerged adopting a Neuro-Symbolic approach, called transformer guided chaining, whereby the idea is to iteratively perform 1-step neural inferences and chain together the results to generate a multi-step reasoning trace. Several works have adapted variants of this central idea and reported significantly high accuracies compared to vanilla LLM’s. In this paper, we perform a critical empirical investigation of the chaining approach on a multi-hop First-Order Logic (FOL) reasoning benchmark. In particular, we develop a reference implementation, called Chainformer, and conduct several experiments to analyze the accuracy, generalization, interpretability, and performance over FOLs. Our findings highlight key strengths and possible current limitations and suggest potential areas for future research in logic reasoning.

papers.title: Circuit Stability Characterizes Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: Can circuit stability characterize and predict generalization in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit stability as a method to assess model performance and shows it can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization.
papers.conclusion: Circuit stability characterizes generalization in language models and provides an actionable way to assess and improve model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit stability predicts length, structural, and compositional generalization in arithmetic reasoning tasks.
Circuit instability in arithmetic indicates lack of understanding of commutativity and associativity.
For Boolean expression evaluation, circuit non-equivalence indicates structural generalization issues.
Chain-of-thought prompting induces circuit stability and improves performance.
Circuit stability is a robust estimator of model performance that can be computed efficiently.
papers.limitation:
Empirical case studies are limited in terms of tasks and models.
Computational cost of circuit discovery can be high for very large models.
Constructing partitions manually requires prior knowledge of the task.
future_direction: Extending circuit stability to other modalities and architectures.
Investigating the connection between circuit stability and generalization bounds.
Automating the construction of partitions for complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Extensively evaluating the capabilities of (large) language models is difficult. Rapid development of state-of-the-art models induce benchmark saturation, while creating more challenging datasets is labor-intensive. Inspired by the recent developments in mechanistic interpretability, we introduce circuit stability as a new way to assess model performance. Circuit stability refers to a model's ability to apply a consistent reasoning process-its circuit-across various inputs. We mathematically formalize circuit stability and circuit equivalence. Then, through three case studies, we empirically show that circuit stability and the lack thereof can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization. Our proposed methods offer a step towards rigorously relating the generality of models to their interpretability.

papers.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully explain the model's actual reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes tests for measuring faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning and finds that faithfulness varies across tasks and model sizes, with smaller models often producing more faithful reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning is not always faithful, but it can be faithful under carefully chosen circumstances such as model size and task. Smaller models may be better to use if faithful reasoning is important.
papers.key_findings:
Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer.
CoT's performance boost does not come from added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT.
As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks studied.
Smaller models often generate more faithful reasoning than larger, more capable ones.
Faithfulness depends on model size and task difficulty, with easier tasks and larger models leading to less faithful reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Lack of ground truth about the model's internal reasoning process, making it impossible to know if CoT is truly faithful.
Analysis limited to RLHF-finetuned models; faithfulness may differ for pretrained LLMs or other training schemes.
future_direction: Investigate training schemes different from RLHF for eliciting more faithful reasoning.
Use the proposed metrics to increase the faithfulness of CoT and build systems with trustworthy reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform better when they produce step-by-step, "Chain-of-Thought" (CoT) reasoning before answering a question, but it is unclear if the stated reasoning is a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning (i.e., its process for answering the question). We investigate hypotheses for how CoT reasoning may be unfaithful, by examining how the model predictions change when we intervene on the CoT (e.g., by adding mistakes or paraphrasing it). Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer, sometimes relying heavily on the CoT and other times primarily ignoring it. CoT's performance boost does not seem to come from CoT's added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT. As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks we study. Overall, our results suggest that CoT can be faithful if the circumstances such as the model size and task are carefully chosen.

papers.title: Disentangling Memory and Reasoning Ability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle memory recall and reasoning steps in large language models to improve performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel LLM inference paradigm that disentangles memory recall and reasoning steps using special tokens, enhancing both accuracy and interpretability in complex QA tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed decomposition of memory and reasoning steps in LLMs leads to improved performance and greater interpretability, enabling better error analysis and model refinement.
papers.key_findings:
The method improves LLM performance on StrategyQA, CommonsenseQA, and TruthfulQA benchmarks, outperforming baselines like CoT and planning tokens.
On TruthfulQA, the enhanced LLaMA-3.1-8B model achieves 86.6% accuracy, surpassing GPT-4o with CoT prompting.
Error analysis reveals that most errors originate from reasoning steps rather than memory recall, highlighting reasoning as the primary challenge.
The decomposition enhances interpretability by allowing clear separation of memory and reasoning steps in the inference process.
Attention analysis shows that special tokens receive higher attention weights, indicating their role in guiding knowledge and reasoning content generation.
papers.limitation:
Dependency on training data quality for memory recall
Token utilization complexity due to special tokens
Performance may struggle with highly complex reasoning tasks
Computation overhead from decomposing steps
future_direction: Dynamic memory updating to incorporate new information without retraining.
Adaptive reasoning steps based on task complexity.
Interpretable error analysis tools for tracing failures to memory or reasoning steps.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in handling complex tasks requiring both extensive knowledge and reasoning abilities. However, the existing LLM inference pipeline operates as an opaque process without explicit separation between knowledge retrieval and reasoning steps, making the model's decision-making process unclear and disorganized. This ambiguity can lead to issues such as hallucinations and knowledge forgetting, which significantly impact the reliability of LLMs in high-stakes domains. In this paper, we propose a new inference paradigm that decomposes the complex inference process into two distinct and clear actions: (1) memory recall: which retrieves relevant knowledge, and (2) reasoning: which performs logical steps based on the recalled knowledge. To facilitate this decomposition, we introduce two special tokens memory and reason, guiding the model to distinguish between steps that require knowledge retrieval and those that involve reasoning. Our experiment results show that this decomposition not only improves model performance but also enhances the interpretability of the inference process, enabling users to identify sources of error and refine model responses effectively. The code is available at https://github.com/MingyuJ666/Disentangling-Memory-and-Reasoning.

papers.title: Change of Thought: Adaptive Test-Time Computation
papers.research_question: How can we boost the expressive power of encoder Transformers without resorting to token-level autoregression?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the SELF-Transformer, an encoder layer that iteratively refines its own attention weights to a fixed point, enabling adaptive test-time computation and improving performance without increasing parameter count.
papers.conclusion: SELF-Transformer recovers much of the expressive power of iterative reasoning while preserving the simplicity of pure encoder architectures, demonstrating substantial benefits from input-adaptive alignment at test time.
papers.key_findings:
SELF-Transformer achieves up to 20% accuracy gains on encoder-style benchmarks without increasing parameter count.
On the induction head task, SELF-Transformer achieves 91.1% accuracy compared to 63.1% for a standard Transformer.
On language benchmarks (GLUE, SQuAD, WikiText2), SELF-Transformer outperforms baseline models like BERT-base and RoBERTa-base.
On image classification (ImageNet-1K), SELF-ViT achieves 86.3% top-1 accuracy, outperforming ViT and EfficientNet-B7.
On vision-language tasks, SELF-VLTransformer achieves competitive performance on VQA and retrieval tasks.
papers.limitation:
Computational overhead can arise if the fixed-point iteration requires a high number of steps.
Need for further investigation on generalization capabilities and scaling properties across a wider array of complex tasks, deeper architectures, and longer sequences.
The current implementation does not directly return the iteration count for incorporating an explicit ponder cost for regularization.
future_direction: Adaptation and integration of SELF attention into Large Language Models (LLMs).
Development of more computationally efficient fixed-point solvers and advanced convergence control strategies.
Moving towards explicit and learnable pondering schemes and deeper theoretical understanding of the iterative process.
papers.abstract: Transformers evaluated in a single, fixed-depth pass are provably limited in expressive power to the constant-depth circuit class TC0. Running a Transformer autoregressively removes that ceiling -- first in next-token prediction and, more recently, in chain-of-thought reasoning. Both regimes rely on feedback loops that decode internal states into tokens only to re-encode them in subsequent steps. While this "thinking aloud" mirrors human reasoning, biological brains iterate without externalising intermediate states as language. To boost the expressive power of encoder Transformers without resorting to token-level autoregression, we introduce the SELF-Transformer: an encoder layer that iteratively refines its own attention weights to a fixed point. Instead of producing -- in one pass -- the alignment matrix that remixes the input sequence, the SELF-Transformer iteratively updates that matrix internally, scaling test-time computation with input difficulty. This adaptivity yields up to 20\% accuracy gains on encoder-style benchmarks without increasing parameter count, demonstrating that input-adaptive alignment at test time offers substantial benefits for only a modest extra compute budget. Self-Transformers thus recover much of the expressive power of iterative reasoning while preserving the simplicity of pure encoder architectures.

papers.title: Weight-sparse transformers have interpretable circuits
papers.research_question: Does training weight-sparse transformers lead to more interpretable circuits? How does sparsity trade off with capability and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Training weight-sparse transformers leads to interpretable circuits with neurons and residual channels corresponding to natural concepts. Sparsity trades off capability for interpretability, and scaling model size improves this trade-off.
papers.conclusion: Weight-sparse transformers enable the discovery of highly interpretable circuits, validated by rigorous ablation, though scaling sparse models remains a challenge.
papers.key_findings:
Weight-sparse models yield circuits that are roughly 16-fold smaller than dense models of comparable pretraining loss.
Circuits in sparse models are necessary and sufficient for task performance, as shown by ablation studies.
Scaling total parameter count improves the capability-interpretability Pareto frontier.
Qualitative analysis reveals interpretable algorithms for tasks like string closing, bracket counting, and variable type tracking.
Preliminary results show that bridges can be used to extract circuits from existing dense models.
papers.limitation:
Scaling sparse models beyond tens of millions of nonzero parameters while preserving interpretability remains a challenge.
Sparse models are extremely inefficient to train and deploy, and are unlikely to ever reach frontier capabilities.
The use of mean ablation for circuit validation is a weaker form of faithfulness compared to full causal scrubbing.
future_direction: Pushing circuit faithfulness to full causal scrubbing and beyond.
Scaling up sparse models with systems optimizations.
Applying the bridge method more extensively to explain existing dense models.
papers.abstract: Finding human-understandable circuits in language models is a central goal of the field of mechanistic interpretability. We train models to have more understandable circuits by constraining most of their weights to be zeros, so that each neuron only has a few connections. To recover fine-grained circuits underlying each of several hand-crafted tasks, we prune the models to isolate the part responsible for the task. These circuits often contain neurons and residual channels that correspond to natural concepts, with a small number of straightforwardly interpretable connections between them. We study how these models scale and find that making weights sparser trades off capability for interpretability, and scaling model size improves the capability-interpretability frontier. However, scaling sparse models beyond tens of millions of nonzero parameters while preserving interpretability remains a challenge. In addition to training weight-sparse models de novo, we show preliminary results suggesting our method can also be adapted to explain existing dense models. Our work produces circuits that achieve an unprecedented level of human understandability and validates them with considerable rigor.

papers.title: ThoughtProbe: Classifier-Guided Thought Space Exploration Leveraging LLM Intrinsic Reasoning
papers.research_question: How are reasoning capabilities represented within LLMs’ internal activations, and how can these intrinsic abilities be effectively harnessed?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ThoughtProbe, a classifier-guided search framework that leverages linear separability of thoughtfulness in LLM activations to improve reasoning performance without human intervention.
papers.conclusion: ThoughtProbe effectively leverages LLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities through classifier-guided exploration, advancing understanding and enabling practical application without human intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Thoughtfulness is linearly separable in LLMs' activation space, with a simple linear classifier achieving over 80% performance.
Different LLMs encode thoughtfulness differently across representation types and layers.
The classifier's logit consistently assigns higher scores to correct, thoughtful responses regardless of length.
The ThoughtProbe framework outperforms baselines on multiple math reasoning benchmarks.
Branch-aggregation selection outperforms single-branch selection and majority voting.
papers.limitation:
Fixed token lengths for segmenting intermediate thoughts may disrupt natural reasoning.
The gap between coverage and accuracy suggests room for improvement in answer selection.
Misalignment between training objectives (final outcomes) and guidance criteria (intermediate progress) may limit effectiveness.
future_direction: Explore more flexible, semantic-aware splitting criteria for tree node expansion.
Develop more sophisticated scoring metrics and aggregation methods for answer selection.
Explore step-wise feedback or hierarchical evaluation to better align classifier training.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have been demonstrated to possess intrinsic reasoning capabilities that can emerge naturally when expanding the response space. However, the neural representation mechanisms underlying these intrinsic capabilities and approaches for their optimal utilization remain inadequately understood. In this work, we make the key discovery that a simple linear classifier can effectively detect intrinsic reasoning capabilities in LLMs' activation space, particularly within specific representation types and network layers. Based on this finding, we propose a classifier-guided search framework that strategically explore a tree-structured response space. In each node expansion, the classifier serves as a scoring and ranking mechanism that efficiently allocates computational resources by identifying and prioritizing more thoughtful reasoning directions for continuation. After completing the tree expansion, we collect answers from all branches to form a candidate answer pool. We propose a branch-aggregation selection method that marginalizes over all supporting branches by aggregating their thoughtfulness scores, thereby identifying the optimal answer from the pool. Experimental results show that our framework's comprehensive exploration not only covers valid reasoning chains but also effectively identifies them, achieving significant improvements across multiple arithmetic reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: REFINER: Reasoning Feedback on Intermediate Representations
papers.research_question: How does interacting with fine-grained reasoning feedback on intermediate reasoning steps impact the performance of language models on reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REFINER, a framework where a generator LM iteratively refines its intermediate reasoning steps using structured feedback from a critic model, leading to improved performance on reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: REFINER demonstrates that structured, fine-grained feedback on intermediate reasoning errors significantly improves LM performance on reasoning tasks, and the critic model can serve as a reasoning refinement tool for LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
REFINER significantly outperforms baseline LMs of comparable scale on three diverse reasoning tasks (math word problems, synthetic natural language reasoning, and moral action generation).
The trained critic model alone can improve the reasoning of large LMs like GPT-3.5 without fine-tuning the reasoner.
Structured, fine-grained feedback is more beneficial for improving reasoning than scalar value feedback (e.g., from automatic metrics like BLEU).
Improving the generation of intermediate representations leads to better performance on the final answer prediction.
Training a generator with an imperfect (noisy) critic is still beneficial for performance.
papers.limitation:
The framework is not evaluated on all applicable downstream reasoning tasks due to their sheer number.
The critic model is task-specific, while an ideal critic would be general and capable of providing feedback on a wide range of reasoning tasks.
The considered fine-grained reasoning error types are specific to the chosen tasks and do not cover all possible error types.
future_direction: Generalizing the critic model to be capable of providing feedback on a wide range of reasoning tasks.
Generalizing the fine-grained reasoning error types beyond the tasks considered.
papers.abstract: Debjit Paul, Mete Ismayilzada, Maxime Peyrard, Beatriz Borges, Antoine Bosselut, Robert West, Boi Faltings. Proceedings of the 18th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Large-Scale Counting in LLMs through a System-2 Strategy
papers.research_question: How can a test-time strategy inspired by System-2 cognitive processes overcome the architectural limitations of LLMs in large-scale counting tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a simple test-time strategy that decomposes large counting tasks into smaller sub-problems, enabling LLMs to surpass their architectural limitations and achieve high accuracy, and provides a mechanistic interpretation of how this System-2-like strategy functions within the models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed System-2 test-time strategy effectively overcomes the architectural limitations of LLMs in large-scale counting by decomposing the task, and mechanistic analysis reveals how count information is stored, transferred, and aggregated within the model.
papers.key_findings:
A System-2 strategy combining structured input (partitioning with a separator) and intermediate reasoning steps (Chain-of-Thought) enables LLMs to accurately count large numbers of items, overcoming the performance degradation seen in standard (System-1) counting.
Attention analysis shows that during intermediate reasoning, the model attends strongly to the final item/separator of each partition in middle-to-late layers (e.g., layers 19-23), and during final answer generation, it attends to the intermediate count tokens.
Causal mediation analysis (activation patching) identifies that count information is stored in the final item representations of each partition, transferred via specific attention heads, and aggregated to produce the final total.
The model's internal counting mechanism (System-1) is capacity-limited and degrades for counts beyond approximately 30 items due to transformer depth constraints, explaining the failure on large-scale counting.
Neither structured input alone nor Chain-of-Thought reasoning alone is sufficient for accurate large-scale counting; their combination is necessary.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on a narrow counting task with limited object diversity, using simple repeated nouns in synthetic contexts.
The approach depends on structured prompts and assumes prior knowledge of the model's reliable counting range, which may limit generalization.
The effects of tokenization and number representation are not isolated and may independently influence the results.
future_direction: Explore further applications of this strategy to complex reasoning tasks in language and beyond.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite strong performance on complex mathematical problems, exhibit systematic limitations in counting tasks. This issue arises from architectural limits of transformers, where counting is performed across layers, leading to degraded precision for larger counting problems due to depth constraints. To address this limitation, we propose a simple test-time strategy inspired by System-2 cognitive processes that decomposes large counting tasks into smaller, independent sub-problems that the model can reliably solve. We evaluate this approach using observational and causal mediation analyses to understand the underlying mechanism of this System-2-like strategy. Our mechanistic analysis identifies key components: latent counts are computed and stored in the final item representations of each part, transferred to intermediate steps via dedicated attention heads, and aggregated in the final stage to produce the total count. Experimental results demonstrate that this strategy enables LLMs to surpass architectural limitations and achieve high accuracy on large-scale counting tasks. This work provides mechanistic insight into System-2 counting in LLMs and presents a generalizable approach for improving and understanding their reasoning behavior.

papers.title: Adaptive Circuit Behavior and Generalization in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How well does the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small generalize to prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of its algorithm?
papers.core_contribution: The IOI circuit generalizes surprisingly well to prompt variants, reusing all its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges, and a mechanism called S2 Hacking explains how the circuit outperforms the full model on these variants.
papers.conclusion: The IOI circuit in GPT-2 small generalizes more effectively than previously understood, reusing its core components and mechanisms while adapting through minimal structural changes, offering insights into the broader capabilities of large neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The base IOI circuit outperforms the full model on DoubleIO and TripleIO prompt variants where the IOI algorithm would fail.
A mechanism termed S2 Hacking explains how the circuit achieves high performance on these variants by focusing on the S2 token due to the knockout procedure.
New circuits discovered for DoubleIO and TripleIO variants reuse all components of the base IOI circuit, only adding edges from additional input tokens (IO2 for DoubleIO, IO2 and IO3 for TripleIO).
The circuit components (attention heads) largely retain their functionalities from the base IOI task when evaluated on the variants.
The order of names in the prompt affects performance, with a 'first come, first serve' mechanism observed in a Previous Token head (2.2).
future_direction: a more detailed study of the duplicate suppression mechanism
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the inner workings of large neural networks by identifying circuits, or minimal subgraphs within the model that implement algorithms responsible for performing specific tasks. These circuits are typically discovered and analyzed using a narrowly defined prompt format. However, given the abilities of large language models (LLMs) to generalize across various prompt formats for the same task, it remains unclear how well these circuits generalize. For instance, it is unclear whether the models generalization results from reusing the same circuit components, the components behaving differently, or the use of entirely different components. In this paper, we investigate the generality of the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small, which is well-studied and believed to implement a simple, interpretable algorithm. We evaluate its performance on prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of this algorithm. Our findings reveal that the circuit generalizes surprisingly well, reusing all of its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges. Notably, the circuit generalizes even to prompt variants where the original algorithm should fail; we discover a mechanism that explains this which we term S2 Hacking. Our findings indicate that circuits within LLMs may be more flexible and general than previously recognized, underscoring the importance of studying circuit generalization to better understand the broader capabilities of these models.

papers.title: Autoregressive + Chain of Thought = Recurrent: Recurrence's Role in Language Models' Computability and a Revisit of Recurrent Transformer
papers.research_question: What are the distinct roles of recurrence and autoregression in neural models' computational power, and how does Chain of Thought (CoT) approximate recurrence to enhance reasoning capabilities in Transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that recurrence is crucial for computational depth in neural models, and that Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting approximates this missing recurrence in autoregressive Transformers by converting hidden states to text and back, thereby enhancing their computational capabilities. It also introduces the concept of 'recurrence-completeness' to analyze recurrent Transformer variants.
papers.conclusion: The analysis clarifies the roles of autoregression and recurrence, showing recurrence is key for computational depth. CoT approximates recurrence in Transformers, boosting their reasoning. The concept of recurrence-completeness reveals that some recurrent Transformer designs prioritize speed over computational power.
papers.key_findings:
Recurrence, not autoregression, is essential for increasing the depth complexity of neural models, enabling them to solve tasks requiring sequential computation.
Chain of Thought (CoT) mimics recurrence in Transformer-based LLMs by encoding hidden computational states into natural language tokens and decoding them back, acting as a bridge between autoregression and recurrence.
Empirical results show that CoT-enhanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) can solve tasks at Regular, Context-Free, and Context-Sensitive computational levels, whereas standard Transformers without CoT fail.
Some 'recurrent' Transformer designs (e.g., Linear Transformer, RWKV) are recurrence-incomplete and do not enhance computational power; they primarily aim for inference efficiency.
There is a trade-off between recurrence-completeness and parallel training: true recurrent models cannot be parallelized, while recurrence-incomplete models like Linear Transformers can.
papers.limitation:
Experimental task lengths are limited to under 20 elements to avoid issues with long-context retrieval and model errors unrelated to computability, which may limit generalizability to longer sequences.
The study uses only one LLM (GPT-4) for experiments, which may not represent all language models.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture excels in a variety of language modeling tasks, outperforming traditional neural architectures such as RNN and LSTM. This is partially due to its elimination of recurrent connections, which allows for parallel training and a smoother flow of gradients. However, this move away from recurrent structures places the Transformer model at the lower end of Chomsky's computational hierarchy, imposing limitations on its computational abilities. Consequently, even advanced Transformer-based models face considerable difficulties in tasks like counting, string reversal, and multiplication. These tasks, though seemingly elementary, require a level of computational complexity that exceeds the capabilities of the Transformer architecture. Concurrently, the emergence of ``Chain of Thought" (CoT) prompting has enabled Transformer-based language models to tackle tasks that were previously impossible or poorly executed. In this work, we thoroughly investigate the influence of recurrent structures in neural models on their reasoning abilities and computability, contrasting the role autoregression plays in the neural models' computational power. We then shed light on how the CoT approach can mimic recurrent computation and act as a bridge between autoregression and recurrence in the context of language models. It is this approximated recurrence that notably improves the model's performance and computational capacity. Moreover, we revisit recent recurrent-based Transformer model designs, focusing on their computational abilities through our proposed concept of ``recurrence-completeness" and identify key theoretical limitations in models like Linear Transformer and RWKV. Through this, we aim to provide insight into the neural model architectures and prompt better model design.

papers.title: Lost in Transmission: When and Why LLMs Fail to Reason Globally
papers.research_question: What causes LLMs to fail on tasks requiring complex reasoning over large parts of their input? The paper hypothesizes that these failures are due to capacity limits on the accurate flow of information (effective bandwidth) within LLMs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the BAPO model to explain LLM failures on global reasoning tasks due to limited effective bandwidth, and shows that chain of thought can mitigate these limitations.
papers.conclusion: The BAPO model explains LLM failures on global reasoning tasks due to limited effective bandwidth, and chain of thought is an effective mitigation. Future work includes developing architectures and inference methods to overcome bandwidth limits.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs struggle with BAPO-hard problems (e.g., REACHABILITY, MAJORITY) even on relatively small instances.
LLMs perform well on BAPO-easy problems (e.g., INDEX, EQUALITY) across input lengths.
Chain of thought reasoning can transform BAPO-hard problems into BAPO-easy steps, enabling constant-bandwidth BAPOs to solve any decidable problem.
Empirical results confirm that adding chain of thought improves performance on BAPO-hard problems, but limited CoT budgets still lead to performance drops.
The BAPO model provides a principled explanation for LLM failures on global reasoning tasks and suggests mitigation strategies.
papers.limitation:
Our BAPO model abstracts away many details of the transformer architecture, which may miss important nuances.
Our empirical evaluation is limited to a set of synthetic tasks and two real-world tasks; future work should test on a broader set.
Our study focuses on single-token output problems, while many real-world tasks require longer outputs.
We assume that the effective bandwidth is constant, but in practice it might vary with input length or model scale.
future_direction: Developing architectures and inference methods that mitigate bandwidth limits.
Testing on a broader set of real-world tasks.
Extending the BAPO model to multi-token outputs and other architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite their many successes, transformer-based large language models (LLMs) continue to struggle with tasks that require complex reasoning over large parts of their input. We argue that these failures arise due to capacity limits on the accurate flow of information within LLMs. To formalize this issue, we introduce the bounded attention prefix oracle (BAPO) model, a new computational framework that models bandwidth constraints on attention heads, the mechanism for internal communication in LLMs. We show that several important reasoning problems like graph reachability require high communication bandwidth for BAPOs to solve; we call these problems BAPO-hard. Our experiments corroborate our theoretical predictions: GPT-4o, Claude, and Gemini succeed on BAPO-easy tasks and fail even on relatively small BAPO-hard tasks. BAPOs also reveal another benefit of chain of thought (CoT): we prove that breaking down a task using CoT can turn any BAPO-hard problem into a BAPO-easy one. Our results offer principled explanations for key LLM failures and suggest directions for architectures and inference methods that mitigate bandwidth limits.

papers.title: Small transformer architectures for task switching
papers.research_question: Whether attention-based architectures (transformers) outperform traditional approaches (MLPs, RNNs) for small-scale applications, specifically in the context of task switching.
papers.core_contribution: Standard transformers do not outperform MLPs or LSTMs on a basic task switching benchmark (IARC), but a combination of a non-translationally invariant transformer (cisformer) and an alternative attention mechanism (expressive attention) achieves high performance (~95% accuracy).
papers.conclusion: The combination of cisformer and expressive attention is the only model able to achieve substantial performance on the basic IARC task, indicating that the workings of attention can be understood better and improved by comparing different formulations in task-switching settings.
papers.key_findings:
Standard transformers, MLPs, and LSTMs achieve similar, modest prediction accuracies (~45%) on the full IARC task.
The cisformer (non-translationally invariant transformer) with expressive attention is the only model achieving substantial performance (~95%) on the IARC task.
Expressive attention improves performance over standard dot-product attention in both standard transformers and cisformers.
The cisformer with standard dot-product attention does not outperform MLPs or LSTMs.
future_direction: Extend the IARC framework for larger models and more elaborated task switching frameworks.
Reformulate the attention mechanism based on the insights from expressive attention.
papers.abstract: The rapid progress seen in terms of large-scale generative AI is largely based on the attention mechanism. It is conversely non-trivial to conceive small-scale applications for which attention-based architectures outperform traditional approaches, such as multi-layer perceptrons or recurrent networks. We examine this problem in the context of 'task switching'. In this framework models work on ongoing token sequences with the current task being determined by stochastically interspersed control tokens. We show that standard transformers cannot solve a basic task switching reference model based on finite domain arithmetics which contains subtasks dedicated to increment / addition / reverse copy / context (IARC). We show that transformers, long short-term memory recurrent networks (LSTM), and plain multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) achieve similar, but only modest prediction accuracies. We enlarge our comparative study by including an extension of the standard transformer architecture to its non-translational invariant counterpart, the cisformer, and an alternative attention mechanism, extensive attention. A combination of the latter is found to be the only model able to achieve considerable performance levels, of around 95%. Our results indicate that the workings of attention can be understood better, and even improved, when comparing qualitatively different formulations in task-switching settings.

papers.title: Beyond Chains of Thought: Benchmarking Latent-Space Reasoning Abilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the internal reasoning abilities (reasoning leaps) of large language models, and to what extent do they engage in complex latent-space computations without explicit token generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark to quantify latent-space reasoning leaps in LLMs, demonstrating that LLMs can perform internal reasoning and that performance varies across models and reasoning domains.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can perform latent-space reasoning, and larger dense models may have greater potential for internal reasoning, which has implications for safety and the need to monitor opaque internal computations.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-4.5 achieves the highest accuracy (74.7%) on the benchmark, outperforming other models like Grok-2 and Llama 3.1 405B.
Smaller models generally perform worse than larger models, but there are exceptions (e.g., Llama 3.1 70B and 405B perform similarly).
Models with MoE architectures (e.g., Llama 4 Maverick, DeepSeek-V3) underperform compared to dense models of similar total parameter count.
Performance varies across reasoning domains, with social, spatial, and temporal reasoning being more challenging than arithmetic, causal, logical, moral, and linguistic reasoning.
Control experiments suggest that models are not merely exploiting heuristics in the main benchmark, but are actually reasoning internally.
papers.limitation:
Models may exploit heuristics rather than engage in genuine reasoning, which is a limitation of the benchmark.
The benchmark cannot reliably determine when models shift from reasoning to heuristic-based strategies.
